text: SOC Operations & SIEM Fundamentals introduced MTTD, mean time to detect, and MTTR, mean time to respond. Those metrics aren't new here. What's new is how they get used in Post-Incident Activity — not as a single number calculated once a quarter, but recorded per-incident and tracked as a trend across similar incidents over time, because every incident is different and one data point proves nothing on its own.

Picture three business email compromise incidents over a few months. Incident one: MTTD 38 minutes, MTTR 4 hours 10 minutes, including the hour lost confirming MFA status. Incident two, after the access fix and playbook change landed: MTTD 35 minutes, MTTR 2 hours 5 minutes — that MFA check now takes under five minutes. Incident three: MTTD 29 minutes, MTTR 1 hour 50 minutes, helped by the new Sentinel rule catching a related attempt early.

That trend line is real evidence the meeting, the report, and the new rule weren't paperwork. But a trend only answers whether things got faster, not whether the team actually did what it said it would. That requires going back to the after-action report's action items and checking each one against its named owner and deadline — did the access actually get granted, did the playbook actually get updated.

An after-action report with action items nobody ever re-checks is exactly as useless as one with no action items at all. Verifying completion is what makes Post-Incident Activity a closed loop instead of a one-time exercise in writing things down. Put together, this chapter is a meeting surfacing problems, a report assigning owned fixes, a rule making one permanent, and this lesson confirming it all actually worked.

That's the exact Preparation-to-Preparation cycle from Chapter 1, now fully worked through with real evidence instead of just a diagram. With Post-Incident Activity closed out, the course turns from reacting to confirmed incidents toward going looking for attackers nobody has alerted on yet — starting with hypothesis-driven threat hunting.
